entities.name: Human Prehistory
entities.summary: From the earliest stone toolmaking to the first written records. Dated by measurement rather than reckoning, so quoted in years before present.
entities.date_note: SCOPE GATE. This app begins where human-like BEHAVIOUR begins, not where a taxon does. The floor is the earliest knapped stone — currently Lomekwi 3 at 3.3 Ma, which predates the oldest Homo fossil by about 500,000 years. A taxonomic floor would exclude the oldest instance of the very behaviour this app exists to track, and taxonomy is the least stable line available: H. habilis placement is disputed and the Ledi-Geraru mandible is unnamed. Knapping is the line rather than tool use, because tool use extends to chimpanzees and orangutans and so runs past the ~7 Ma common ancestor, which would make any floor arbitrary. The end is diachronous: writing appears at different times in different regions.

caveats.text: The floor is a behaviour, not a site. If an older knapping site is accepted, this date moves and the app's scope does not change.

entities.name: Hominins
entities.summary: Humans, proto-humans and near-humans: a dozen or so named species, most of which overlapped with others rather than succeeding them in a line.
entities.date_note: The earliest fossil attributed to Homo is LD 350-1 from Ledi-Geraru, Ethiopia, at 2.80-2.75 Ma, constrained by the Gurumaha Tuff at 2.782 +/- 0.006 Ma. The genus is ongoing, so it outlasts prehistory rather than ending with it.

alternatives.label: LD 350-1 not assignable to Homo
alternatives.note: Argues the mandible cannot be unequivocally attributed to Homo, which would leave the genus with no securely dated fossil this early.

entities.name: Homo habilis
entities.date_note: Whether the material forms one species, and whether it belongs in Homo at all, is still argued. The late specimen KNM-ER 42703 is 1.44 Ma.

caveats.text: Some researchers would move this material out of Homo entirely, which would change where our genus begins.

entities.summary: An early, small-brained human in Africa from about 2.4 to 1.4 million years ago, overlapping with other human species.

entities.name: Homo rudolfensis
entities.date_note: Type specimen KNM-ER 1470, Koobi Fora. Four hominin species coexisted in the Turkana Basin between 2.0 and 1.5 Ma.

caveats.text: Some researchers assign this material to Homo habilis rather than to a separate species.

entities.summary: A flat-faced, big-toothed early human from Kenya about 1.9 million years ago whose place in the human genus is still argued over.

entities.name: Homo erectus
entities.date_note: Treated here sensu lato, including African material sometimes separated as H. ergaster. The terminal Ngandong date rests on Bayesian modelling of 52 radiometric estimates.
entities.summary: The first widely travelled human species, present from about 1.9 million years ago until roughly 110,000 years ago in Java.

entities.name: Homo antecessor
entities.date_note: Gran Dolina level TD6 dates to 780-857 ka. The young limit is fixed by reversed Matuyama polarity, which requires an age greater than 780 ka.
entities.summary: An early European human from a Spanish cave, about 800,000 years old, whose status as a separate species is still argued.

entities.name: Homo heidelbergensis
entities.date_note: Range may reach 1.3 Ma if older Spanish and Italian material is included.

caveats.text: Functions partly as a catch-all for Middle Pleistocene humans; several proposed splits would dismantle it.

entities.summary: A large-brained Middle Pleistocene human in Europe, Africa and the Near East, roughly 700,000 to 200,000 years ago.

entities.name: Homo naledi
entities.date_note: Its position in the human family tree is unresolved.
entities.summary: A small-brained human found deep in a South African cave system, surprisingly recent at 335,000 to 236,000 years ago.

entities.name: Homo neanderthalensis
entities.date_note: No method is stated for the 400 ka appearance. The END is radiocarbon: the associated Mousterian closes 41,030-39,260 cal BP by AMS with Bayesian modelling across 40 sites. Radiocarbon cannot reach the start, so the two boundaries rest on different evidence.
entities.summary: Cold-adapted humans across Europe and western Asia, from about 400,000 years ago until roughly 40,000 years ago.

entities.name: Denisovans
entities.date_note: Genetically unambiguous but with no formally accepted species name and no type specimen in the conventional sense. The chronology is a Bayesian model combining radiocarbon, uranium-series and luminescence ages, so no single method describes it; radiocarbon alone cannot reach 195 ka.
entities.summary: A human population known mainly from DNA, identified from fragments in a Siberian cave and traceable in living people.

entities.name: Homo floresiensis
entities.date_note: Skeletal remains to about 60 ka, associated artefacts from about 190 ka and continuing to about 50 ka.

alternatives.label: Original 2004 chronology
alternatives.note: Withdrawn in 2016: the dated deposits proved to be a younger unit unconformably overlying the remains.

caveats.text: Often reported as surviving until 12,000 years ago. That date was corrected to around 60,000 in 2016.

entities.summary: A small-bodied human on the Indonesian island of Flores, known from Liang Bua cave.

entities.name: Homo luzonensis
entities.date_note: Minimum age revised upward to at least 134 ka in 2023. No youngest-remains date is established; the original 67 ka metatarsal age is now read as a minimum from the dating method rather than a true age.
entities.summary: A human species known from a handful of bones and teeth in a cave on Luzon, the Philippines.

entities.name: Homo sapiens
entities.date_note: 315 +/- 34 ka is the thermoluminescence age of heated flints with the Jebel Irhoud hominins in Morocco. Which fossils count as H. sapiens is itself part of the disagreement about the date.
entities.summary: Our own species, first recognisable in Africa around 300,000 years ago.

entities.name: Homo longi
entities.date_note: Known from one cranium with a minimum U-series age of about 146 ka, so there is no species-level range.

alternatives.label: Harbin cranium is Denisovan
alternatives.note: Palaeoproteomic analysis in 2025 recovered 95 endogenous proteins and clustered the specimen with Denisova 3.

caveats.text: Named as a new species in 2021; 2025 protein evidence indicates the specimen is a Denisovan.

entities.summary: A single large skull from Harbin, China, whose identity was overturned by protein analysis in 2025.

entities.name: Oldowan Industry
entities.date_note: Usually given as 2.6-1.7 Ma. Older claims exist, but the 3.3 Ma Lomekwi 3 tools are excluded by classifying them as Lomekwian, so the boundary is definitional as much as evidential.
entities.summary: The earliest widely recognised stone tools: sharp flakes struck from pebble cores.

entities.name: Acheulean Industry
entities.date_note: Earliest at Kokiselei 4, West Turkana, Kenya, at 1.76 Ma — about 350,000 years earlier than previously accepted. The end is diffuse rather than dated.
entities.summary: The handaxe tradition: teardrop-shaped tools worked on both faces, made for well over a million years.

entities.name: Mousterian Industry
entities.date_note: Hard to separate from the latest Acheulean at the start, so the beginning is definitional and no single method fixes it. The end differs by region and by method, and is radiocarbon where it can be reached.
entities.summary: The flake-tool tradition associated mainly with Neanderthals across Europe and western Asia.

entities.name: Aterian Industry
entities.date_note: 145 +/- 9 ka is the weighted-mean thermoluminescence age at El Mnasra. The industry is defined by tool shape rather than by date, so its limits move with the definition.
entities.summary: A North African tradition marked by tanged points, made by early modern humans across the Sahara.

entities.name: Still Bay Industry
entities.date_note: Single-grain OSL makes this a short episode of under 5,000 years.

alternatives.label: Diepkloof thermoluminescence chronology
alternatives.note: TL at Diepkloof puts the Still Bay some 35,000 years earlier than the single-grain OSL chronology.

entities.summary: A brief South African tradition of finely worked leaf-shaped points, an early flowering of complex technique.

entities.name: Howiesons Poort Industry
entities.date_note: Single-grain OSL makes this a tight horizon marker; ESR and TL at Klasies River give a looser 50,000-60,000 years.

alternatives.label: Klasies River ESR/TL chronology
alternatives.note: Looser and younger than the single-grain OSL horizon.

entities.summary: A South African tradition of small backed blades, hafted as composite tools, lasting only a few thousand years.

entities.name: Later Stone Age
entities.date_note: Border Cave gives 44.2-43.0 cal BP for the earliest layer. There is no real end date: the Later Stone Age runs on into recorded history, and the value here is a convention for the tree rather than a finding.
entities.summary: The sub-Saharan African tradition of small composite tools that continues into the historical period.

entities.name: Châtelperronian Industry
entities.date_note: In Cantabria it shows no chronological overlap with the local Mousterian, which complicates the usual reading of it as a Neanderthal response to arriving modern humans.
entities.summary: A short-lived western European tradition made during the overlap between Neanderthals and modern humans.

entities.name: Aurignacian Industry
entities.date_note: Arrival dates differ sharply between regional models, from about 43 cal ka BP in southern Iberia to later elsewhere.

alternatives.label: Banks et al. 2013 phase model
alternatives.note: Proto-Aurignacian 41.5-39.9 k cal BP, Early Aurignacian 39.8-37.9 k cal BP.

entities.summary: The first widespread modern-human tradition in Europe, associated with the earliest cave art and figurines.

entities.name: Gravettian Industry
entities.date_note: Bayesian boundaries from the Adriatic basin; regional models differ.
entities.summary: The tradition of the Venus figurines and mammoth-bone dwellings, spanning Europe through the coldest part of the Ice Age.

entities.name: Solutrean Industry
entities.date_note: Bayesian analysis does not confirm the traditional ordering of the internal phases, so the sub-sequence is less secure than the overall span.
entities.summary: An Iberian and French tradition known for slender, finely pressure-flaked laurel-leaf points.

entities.name: Magdalenian Industry
entities.date_note: Preceded by the Badegoulian at 23,092-20,792 cal BP. Regional phase models disagree on the internal sequence.
entities.summary: The late Ice Age tradition of Lascaux and Altamira, ending as the glaciers retreated.

entities.name: Göbekli Tepe
entities.date_note: Only 11 radiocarbon dates exist. The Layer III/II/I scheme has been abandoned for at least eight phases, so phase labels in older sources do not map cleanly.
entities.summary: Monumental enclosures raised by people who were not yet farming, in southeastern Anatolia.

entities.name: Monte Verde II
entities.date_note: Under active challenge: a March 2026 reanalysis proposed a Holocene age, roughly thirty specialists rebutted it in May, and the authors replied in June.

alternatives.label: Surovell et al. 2026
alternatives.note: Argues the dated material is intrusive and the occupation is mid-Holocene.

entities.summary: A settlement in southern Chile whose age broke the Clovis-first model of the peopling of the Americas.

entities.name: Behavioural Firsts
entities.summary: The earliest known evidence for each human behaviour — toolmaking, fire, pigment, burial, art, seafaring. Each date is a floor, not an estimate.
entities.date_note: Starts with the contested Dikika cut marks at 3.39 Ma, which is older than the app's 3.3 Ma floor because the floor tracks the oldest ACCEPTED behaviour and Dikika is not accepted.

entities.name: Stone Knapping
entities.date_note: THE SCOPE FLOOR, defined as a behaviour rather than as a site. Lomekwi 3 is the present evidence, not the definition: the artefacts lie above the Toroto Tuff at 3.31 +/- 0.02 Ma, within the Mammoth reverse subchron. If an older knapping site is accepted, this date moves and the app's scope does not change. Predates the oldest Homo fossil by about 500,000 years, which is why the floor is behavioural and not taxonomic.

alternatives.label: Assemblage not in primary context
alternatives.note: Argues the stratigraphic association with the dated tuff is not established. Offers no alternative date; the implied age is essentially the same. The excavators replied in 2019.

caveats.text: A minority reads the flakes as naturally fractured stone rather than deliberate knapping.

entities.summary: The first deliberate shaping of stone into tools — the behaviour this app uses to mark where human prehistory begins.

entities.name: Butchery of Animals
entities.date_note: The secure record begins 2.6-2.5 Ma at Gona and Bouri, Ethiopia. A claim for 3.39 Ma at Dikika is the older candidate and is not accepted.

alternatives.label: Dikika cut marks
alternatives.note: Marks on two bones claimed as butchery before 3.39 Ma. Critics read them as trampling: 96% of experimental trampling grooves are broad and open, against 4% of genuine cut marks.

caveats.text: The 3.39 Ma Dikika claim is widely read as trampling damage rather than butchery.

entities.summary: Cutting meat from bone with stone tools, which opened a food source that had been out of reach.

entities.name: Controlled Use of Fire
entities.date_note: Wonderwerk Cave Stratum 10 is the standard secure minimum, bracketed by cosmogenic burial ages of 1.27 +/- 0.19 and 0.98 +/- 0.19 Ma. Older claims exist and the field has not settled.

alternatives.label: Wonderwerk Stratum 11
alternatives.note: A 2026 reanalysis pushes burning at the same cave back to 1.79-1.07 Ma.

alternatives.label: Gesher Benot Ya'aqov
alternatives.note: The best-evidenced repeated hearth use, fixed by the Matuyama-Brunhes reversal at 0.79 Ma. Younger than Wonderwerk but less contested.

entities.summary: Keeping and using fire on purpose, which changed diet, safety and how far north people could live.

entities.name: Cooking of Food
entities.date_note: Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, from eight sequential horizons correlated to marine isotope stages 18-20. Note the long gap between the earliest fire and the earliest cooking: the two are not the same behaviour.
entities.summary: Applying controlled heat to food, evidenced by fish teeth heated to a temperature that implies cooking rather than burning.

entities.name: Use of Pigment
entities.date_note: Secure from about 300 ka in both Africa and Europe. Between 1.5 Ma and 300 ka the evidence is sparse and equivocal. Kapthurin GnJh-15 in Kenya is the earliest well-dated assemblage at 0.284 +/- 0.012 Ma.

alternatives.label: Olorgesailie worked pigment
alternatives.note: Described as the oldest clearly worked pigment.

entities.summary: Collecting and working coloured earth, the earliest hint of decoration or marking.

entities.name: Deliberate Burial
entities.date_note: Sima de los Huesos in Spain holds over 7,000 bones from at least 29 individuals, a minimum age since the dated speleothem formed directly on the deposit. Whether accumulation counts as burial is the argument. Qafzeh in Israel at 90-100 ka is the earliest undisputed grave.

alternatives.label: Qafzeh, earliest undisputed grave
alternatives.note: A modern-human burial with fallow-deer antlers placed on the chest, cut into bedrock. Thermoluminescence on burnt flint.

alternatives.label: Homo naledi burial claim
alternatives.note: A 2023 claim of deliberate burial by a small-brained hominin at Rising Star, formally rebutted and not accepted.

caveats.text: Whether the Sima accumulation is burial or another process is unresolved; the Homo naledi claim is rejected by most reviewers.

entities.summary: Placing the dead somewhere on purpose rather than leaving them where they fell.

entities.name: Personal Ornaments
entities.date_note: Bizmoune Cave, Morocco: 33 pierced Tritia gibbosula shells, dated by uranium-series on a speleothem to 142,290 +29,300/-22,060 years at 2 sigma. Explicitly a minimum. Single-grain OSL on the same layer gives ages as young as 57,800 +/- 7,200, which is unresolved.

alternatives.label: Bizmoune OSL chronology
alternatives.note: Optically stimulated luminescence on layer 4c returns a far younger age than the uranium-series speleothem date.

entities.summary: Shells pierced and strung to be worn, which means signalling something about yourself to other people.

entities.name: Abstract Engraving
entities.date_note: Blombos Cave, South Africa: 77 +/- 6 ka by thermoluminescence on burnt lithics for the engraved ochre, with a drawn cross-hatch in ochre crayon at about 73 ka from the same site.

alternatives.label: Trinil engraved shell
alternatives.note: A zigzag engraved on a freshwater mussel shell from Java, attributed to Homo erectus. If accepted it moves this threshold back by 350,000 years.

entities.summary: Deliberate cross-hatched patterns cut into ochre — marks that mean something without depicting anything.

entities.name: Intentional Seafaring
entities.date_note: The colonisation of Sahul recorded at Madjedbebe, Australia: 65 +/- 6 ka at 95.4% by single-grain OSL with Bayesian modelling. Reaching Australia required repeated open-water crossings, so the site dates the voyage as well as the landfall.

alternatives.label: Sceptical reading of the Madjedbebe chronology
alternatives.note: Critics read the same OSL data as about 53 +/- 4 ka, arguing artefacts moved down through the sand.

entities.summary: Crossing open water on purpose, out of sight of the far shore, which requires planning and a built craft.

entities.name: Figurative Art
entities.date_note: A narrative scene at Leang Karampuang, Sulawesi: a warty pig with human figures, dated by laser-ablation uranium-series on the overlying carbonate. A minimum, since the art is older than the crust that formed on it. The 2024 laser-ablation method also pushed the neighbouring Leang Bulu' Sipong 4 scene from 44 ka to about 48 ka.

alternatives.label: European Upper Palaeolithic art
alternatives.note: Chauvet's first occupation is 37,000-33,500 cal BP and the Hohle Fels ivory figurine at least 35,000 years old. Long taken as the earliest figurative art until the Sulawesi dates.

caveats.text: Often said to begin in Ice Age Europe. The oldest known figurative art is in Indonesia and predates Chauvet by some 14,000 years.

entities.summary: Pictures of recognisable things — animals and people — rather than patterns.

entities.name: Lomekwian Industry
entities.date_note: Named from Lomekwi 3. Kept separate from the Oldowan because the knapping technique differs, which is also why the Oldowan's 2.6 Ma start is a definitional boundary rather than the start of toolmaking.
entities.summary: The oldest known stone toolkit: large, heavy cores and flakes struck with techniques unlike the later Oldowan.

entities.name: Middle Stone Age
entities.date_note: Roughly 300-30 ka, about 270,000 years. The end is regionally staggered. Radiocarbon only reaches the terminal MSA; everything older rests on OSL, TL, ESR and uranium-series, whose ages are quoted as 'BP' but are not radiocarbon and need no calibration.

alternatives.label: Jacobs & Roberts maximum-age chronology
alternatives.note: Single-grain OSL compresses the diagnostic sub-industries into brief horizons; TL and ESR readings stretch them.

entities.summary: The long African toolmaking tradition during which our own species appeared, and with it pigment, beads and engraving.

entities.name: African Prehistory
entities.date_note: Africa holds the whole span. The hominin species themselves sit under Human Prehistory rather than here, because a species is not a region's property; this branch holds African sites and cultures.
entities.summary: The continent where the human story begins, and where it stays for most of its length.

entities.name: Olduvai Gorge
entities.date_note: Bed I begins immediately above the Naabi Ignimbrite at 2.038 +/- 0.005 Ma. The sequence runs up through Beds II to IV. Among the best-constrained chronologies in African prehistory, with errors of a few thousand years.
entities.summary: A Tanzanian ravine cutting through two million years of deposits, the site that made early human archaeology a dated science.

entities.name: Omo Kibish
entities.date_note: Omo I is older than 233 +/- 22 ka, dated by single-crystal Ar/Ar on sanidine from the overlying KHS Tuff. A minimum: no robust maximum age exists. The date changed in 2022 because the anchoring tephra was reidentified, not because the method improved.
entities.summary: The Ethiopian site of Omo I, for decades the oldest known fossil of our own species.

entities.name: Blombos Cave
entities.date_note: Occupation from 98.9 +/- 4.5 ka to a sterile hiatus sand at 67.8 +/- 4.2 ka, on single-grain OSL. TL on burnt lithics agrees within error.
entities.summary: A South African cave holding engraved ochre, shell beads and the oldest known drawing.

entities.name: Klasies River Mouth
entities.date_note: Base dated by uranium-disequilibrium to about 110 ka, the LBS member corresponding to the Last Interglacial. The top of the MSA sequence is beyond the radiocarbon limit, so 50 ka is a floor rather than an end.

caveats.text: The chronology is broadly accepted; what is argued is whether the fragmentary human remains are fully modern.

entities.summary: A South African cave sequence with some of the earliest anatomically modern human remains outside East Africa.

entities.name: Border Cave
entities.date_note: The 200 ka start rests on ESR. The Early Later Stone Age horizon is 44.2-43.0 ka cal BP by AMS radiocarbon. Occupation continues into the Holocene, so the end here is a convention.

alternatives.label: Conventional Later Stone Age onset
alternatives.note: Villa and Beaumont put the LSA onset here at 44-42 ka cal BP, roughly 20,000 years earlier than the conventional figure elsewhere.

entities.summary: A South African site whose sequence runs from the Middle Stone Age into the present, including the earliest Later Stone Age toolkit.

entities.name: Green Sahara
entities.date_note: Onset about 14.5 ka with the Bolling-Allerod warming. Termination is time-transgressive rather than a single event: the northern and eastern Sahara dried after 8-7 ka while other areas stayed wet.

alternatives.label: Abrupt termination
alternatives.note: deMenocal's marine-core reading has the end as an abrupt step; reanalyses argue for a gradual, regionally staggered dry-down.

entities.summary: The window when the Sahara held lakes, rivers and grassland, and people lived across what is now the largest hot desert on Earth.

entities.name: Nabta Playa
entities.date_note: Early Neolithic from 10,800 cal BP; abandoned to hyperaridity at about 6,200 cal BP as the Green Sahara ended.

caveats.text: The cultural chronology is reasonably settled. The claim that the megaliths are astronomically aligned is not.

entities.summary: A seasonal lake basin in the Egyptian Sahara with cattle burials and a megalithic circle, occupied while the desert was green.

entities.name: West Asian Prehistory
entities.date_note: From the Natufian to the end of the Ubaid. Much of the older literature quotes uncalibrated radiocarbon without saying so, which makes published dates for this region roughly a millennium too young when read as calendar years.
entities.summary: Where farming, villages and monumental building appear first, and hand off to Sumer.

entities.name: Natufian Culture
entities.date_note: Early Natufian 13,000-11,500 cal BC, Late Natufian to about 10,000 cal BC.

caveats.text: Often said the Younger Dryas cold snap forced the Natufians into farming. Rejected: no moisture decline, no biome retreat, and the Early-to-Late shift predates it.

entities.summary: Hunter-gatherers of the Levant who settled in one place, built stone houses and buried their dead with ornaments, before anyone farmed.

entities.name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic A
entities.date_note: 9800/9700 to 8800/8700 cal BC in the PPND scheme, from about 800 compiled radiocarbon dates.
entities.summary: The first farming villages, before pottery: round houses, stored grain and communal building.

entities.name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic B
entities.date_note: 8600 to about 6900 cal BC, the end marked with a question mark in the source. The PPNA/PPNB boundary is a typological convention, and it may be a dating artefact: three of PPND's internal breaks fall on steep slopes and plateaus in the calibration curve rather than on changes in settlement.
entities.summary: Rectangular houses, plastered skulls and the first fully domesticated herds of sheep and goats.

entities.name: Çatalhöyük
entities.date_note: East Mound from about 7100 cal BC; occupation ceases 5975-5865 cal BC at 95% probability, from 33 AMS determinations on short-life samples. Mellaart's original 1960s estimate of c. 7100 BC held up against Bayesian modelling.
entities.summary: A densely packed Anatolian town of mud-brick houses entered through the roof, with wall paintings and burials beneath the floors.

entities.name: Halaf Culture
entities.date_note: Proto-Halaf from 6100 cal BC, Early Halaf proper from 5950, Late Halaf ending 5300 cal BC, followed by a Halaf-Ubaid transition.

alternatives.label: Later Halaf end
alternatives.note: Roughly two centuries later than the conventional 5300 cal BC end.

entities.summary: Northern Mesopotamian villages known for finely painted polychrome pottery traded over long distances.

entities.name: Ubaid Period
entities.date_note: Southern Mesopotamia about 6500-3800 BC counting Ubaid 0; the northern sequence is different, roughly 5300-4300 BC. Hands off to the Uruk period. Rests mainly on ceramic seriation rather than a dense radiocarbon series.

caveats.text: No single agreed phase table exists. The term means different things north and south, and published schemes disagree by 300-900 years per boundary.

entities.summary: The long southern Mesopotamian prelude to cities: irrigation, temples on platforms, and the settlement pattern Sumer inherits.

entities.name: Neolithic Jericho
entities.date_note: STORED AS UNCALIBRATED RADIOCARBON. The familiar 'tower built c. 8300 BC' is an uncalibrated figure that the source never labels as such. Compared against calibrated estimates for the same stages it runs 500-900 years too young, so the tower is roughly a millennium older in calendar terms than the usual number suggests. The stage dates are also internally inconsistent: Stage V is older than Stage III despite being later.

caveats.text: Kenyon read the wall and tower as defensive. Bar-Yosef argues they were flood protection and a ritual structure, which would make this not a fortification at all.

entities.summary: The oldest known town wall and stone tower, built by people who farmed but had not yet made pottery.

entities.name: 'Ain Ghazal
entities.date_note: STORED AS UNCALIBRATED RADIOCARBON for the statue horizon. Grissom gives 6750 +/- 80 BC uncalibrated against 7580 +/- 110 BC calibrated for the same material — an 830-year gap, and both numbers circulate widely. Site dates are mixed; the two late aceramic phases cannot be separated radiometrically at all.
entities.summary: A large Jordanian village of the pre-pottery Neolithic, known for lime plaster statues among the oldest large human figures ever made.

entities.name: European Prehistory
entities.date_note: A navigation era. The early boundary follows the oldest securely dated Neanderthal evidence at Sima de los Huesos, which is uranium-series and luminescence work — radiocarbon reaches nowhere near it.
entities.summary: The deep human past of Europe, from Neanderthals and cave art to farming, monuments, and metal-age cultures.

entities.name: Neanderthal Europe
entities.date_note: The 430 ka start is a minimum bound from Sima de los Huesos, dated by uranium-series and luminescence. The end is the 41,030-39,260 cal BP Mousterian boundary, which IS radiocarbon — the two ends of this range rest on different methods, and only one of them is datable by carbon.

alternatives.label: Older Sima chronology
alternatives.note: Earlier speleothem work placed the Sima hominins at roughly 400-600 ka; later work made them about 100,000 years younger.

entities.summary: Neanderthals lived across Europe for hundreds of thousands of years before disappearing after a period of overlap with modern humans.

entities.name: Chauvet Cave Art
entities.date_note: The calibrated radiocarbon model places art and occupation in two phases between about 37 and 28 thousand years ago.

alternatives.label: Stylistic late chronology
alternatives.note: Some scholars date the black drawings to the Solutrean or Gravettian from style, fauna, and stratigraphy rather than charcoal dates.

caveats.text: The debate is radiocarbon versus stylistic dating, not a claim that the cave paintings are fake or undated.

entities.summary: Artists made charcoal drawings in this French cave during two Upper Paleolithic visits.

entities.name: Lascaux Cave Art
entities.date_note: STORED AS UNCALIBRATED RADIOCARBON because the official account mixes conventional BP measurements with calendar-like ranges without consistently labelling them. Do not convert this entry automatically.

alternatives.label: Earlier antler chronology
alternatives.note: Late-1990s AMS antler results supported a roughly 24,000-23,000 BP attribution before the newer LAsCO programme.

entities.summary: This French cave's famous animal paintings were made during a short Upper Paleolithic occupation.

entities.name: Altamira Cave Art
entities.date_note: The oldest bound is a uranium-series minimum age on calcite over art; the younger black-painting boundary is calibrated radiocarbon.

alternatives.label: Downward U-series revision
alternatives.note: A methodological critique argues uranium loss or thorium correction could make the oldest Cantabrian calcite ages too old.

entities.summary: People added painted and engraved images to Altamira in northern Spain over a very long span.

entities.name: Linear Pottery Culture (LBK)
entities.date_note: Bayesian models put the formative start shortly before 5500 cal BC; the conventional 4900 BC ending remains a useful broad boundary rather than a fully modelled terminus.
entities.summary: Europe's first farmers built long timber houses and made band-decorated pottery across a wide central-European belt.

entities.name: Atlantic Megalithic Tradition
entities.date_note: The first monuments are modelled in the late fifth millennium BC. Later Mediterranean revivals mean the tradition did not end as one clean event.
entities.summary: Communities built large stone tombs and monuments along Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts.

entities.name: Stonehenge Construction
entities.date_note: Bayesian modelling dates the first earthwork to 3000-2920 cal BC and the final recorded construction activity to about 1520 cal BC.

alternatives.label: Alternative stone-setting order
alternatives.note: Competing Bayesian models reorder parts of the sarsen and bluestone sequence within the same broad construction interval.

entities.summary: Stonehenge was built and changed in several stages over roughly fifteen centuries.

entities.name: Corded Ware Culture
entities.date_note: The broad span is regionally variable. Bohemian direct dates establish an early presence by 2900 BCE, while different regions end centuries apart.

alternatives.label: Swiss short chronology
alternatives.note: Swiss lake-settlement tree-ring dates restrict Corded Ware there to a shorter 2750-2400 BC span.

entities.summary: A wide European culture known for cord-marked pots and single graves spread from the Rhine to the Baltic.

entities.name: Bell Beaker Culture
entities.date_note: The conventional 2750-1800 BC span summarizes a regionally uneven archaeological and genetic transformation.
entities.summary: Bell-shaped drinking vessels, new burial customs, and large population movements reshaped much of western Europe.

entities.name: Ötzi
entities.date_note: Radiocarbon places Ötzi's death in the late fourth millennium BC; this range records the published calibrated interval rather than treating a death as a long period.
entities.summary: The naturally preserved body of a man who died in the Alps gives a close view of Copper Age life.

entities.name: Central Asian Prehistory
entities.date_note: This navigation era begins with the Denisova Cave sequence and ends after the latest Bronze Age tradition included here.
entities.summary: The deep history of Inner Asia, including early hominins, horse herding, and the Bronze Age steppe networks.

entities.name: Denisova Cave
entities.date_note: The cave sequence combines luminescence, radiocarbon, uranium-series, and genetic evidence; the earliest occupation may reach about 300 ka.
entities.summary: A Siberian cave with a long record of Neanderthals, Denisovans, and modern humans.

entities.name: Botai Culture
entities.date_note: Botai dates to the fourth millennium BC. Evidence for horse milking and management is strong, but its horses are not the ancestors of modern domestic horses.

caveats.text: Botai horse use does not make Botai the direct source of modern domestic horses; ancient-DNA work overturned that popular claim in 2018.

entities.summary: A northern Kazakh settlement tradition famous for early intensive use of horses.

entities.name: Afanasievo Culture
entities.date_note: The culture's third-millennium BC range is based on a refined radiocarbon chronology for the Altai-Sayan region.
entities.summary: An early pastoral culture of the Altai and Minusinsk Basin with strong ties to western steppe populations.

entities.name: Andronovo Culture
entities.date_note: The label covers related regional traditions whose exact limits vary; this stores the broad nineteenth-to-fifteenth-century BC frame.
entities.summary: A Bronze Age network of steppe communities extending across Kazakhstan and southern Siberia.

entities.name: Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex
entities.date_note: The conventional 2200-1700 BC frame summarizes a complex whose individual oasis sequences do not all begin or end together.
entities.summary: An oasis-based Bronze Age culture of Central Asia known for planned settlements, irrigation, and long-distance exchange.

entities.name: Yamnaya Horizon
entities.date_note: The horizon is conventionally dated to about 3300-2350 BC; new genome-wide work refines its internal formation and spread.
entities.summary: Mobile pastoral communities of the Pontic-Caspian steppe whose movements had major effects across Europe and Asia.

entities.name: Incipient Jōmon
entities.date_note: The national framework gives 16,000-11,000 calibrated BP. Regional boundaries can differ substantially.

caveats.text: The popular '13,000 BCE' beginning repeats raw uncalibrated radiocarbon as a calendar date; the secure pottery range is about 16,140-14,920 cal BP.

entities.summary: The earliest Jōmon stage, marked by some of the world's oldest securely dated pottery.

entities.name: Initial Jōmon
entities.date_note: The national framework gives 11,000-7,000 calibrated BP; local sequences are not synchronous.
entities.summary: A long early Jōmon stage when pottery traditions diversified across the Japanese islands.

entities.name: Early Jōmon
entities.date_note: The national framework gives 7,000-5,300 calibrated BP, while regional pottery phases have different boundaries.
entities.summary: A Jōmon stage of growing regional diversity in settlements and pottery styles.

entities.name: Middle Jōmon
entities.date_note: The national framework gives 5,300-4,400 calibrated BP; large regional AMS programmes refine this differently by area.
entities.summary: A Jōmon stage known for large settlements and elaborate pottery in several regions.

entities.name: Late Jōmon
entities.date_note: The national framework gives 4,400-3,300 calibrated BP; the Jōmon-to-Yayoi transition occurred earlier in Kyushu than in northern Honshu.
entities.summary: A later Jōmon stage before the regionally staggered transition to Yayoi farming communities.

entities.name: Final Jōmon
entities.date_note: The framework gives 3,300 to 2,500/2,300 calibrated BP, so the stored end uses the later 2,300 BP national bound.
entities.summary: The final Jōmon stage, ending at different times in different parts of Japan.

entities.name: Chinese Neolithic
entities.date_note: This navigation era uses the widest dated process in this group, Yangtze rice domestication, as its early edge and the Longshan horizon as its late edge.
entities.summary: The long transition in China from foraging to farming villages, regional cultures, towns, and large waterworks.

entities.name: Peiligang Culture
entities.date_note: The core source explicitly gives 9,000-7,000 calibrated years BP; a commonly repeated 5500-4900 BC type-site range does not state its calibration.
entities.summary: An early farming culture of the central Henan plain, associated with millet cultivation and small villages.

entities.name: Yangshao Culture
entities.date_note: The conventional 5000-3000 BC framework is widely used, but Chinese bare-BP chronologies and regional Bayesian models produce a later start in some areas.

alternatives.label: Shangluo Bayesian chronology
alternatives.note: A regional Bayesian model places Yangshao at about 4200-2900 BC, later and shorter than the conventional span.

entities.summary: A major painted-pottery farming tradition of the middle Yellow River valley.

entities.name: Hongshan Culture
entities.date_note: STORED AS UNCALIBRATED RADIOCARBON / UNLABELLED BP. The available sources give only bare BP or 'years ago' dates, and Chinese practice commonly reports radiocarbon that way. Do not convert automatically.

alternatives.label: Classic Hongshan range
alternatives.note: The older standard places Hongshan at 6,000-5,000 BP; 2025 Zhengjiagou work extends the end to 4,800 years ago.

entities.summary: A jade-working and temple-building culture of the West Liao River region in northeast China.

entities.name: Longshan Culture
entities.date_note: The conventional 2600-1900 BC sequence is archaeological and broad; Bayesian analysis finds overlapping regional traditions rather than a single clean succession.

alternatives.label: Haidai Bayesian chronology
alternatives.note: Haidai modelling places the start boundary at 2900-2500 BC and the end at 2100-1700 BC, with cultural overlap.

entities.summary: A late Neolithic tradition of black pottery, walled settlements, and regional change in the Yellow River basin.

entities.name: Liangzhu Culture
entities.date_note: Direct dates on annual plants in dam construction give this culture a particularly strong calibrated chronology of 5,300-4,300 cal BP.
entities.summary: A Yangtze-delta society with a walled centre, jade traditions, and major dams and waterways.

entities.name: Jiahu
entities.date_note: The calibrated site span is about 9,000-7,800 cal BP; a second source renders the occupation as 7000-5700 BC without stating its calibration.
entities.summary: An early Henan village known for rice, bone flutes, and much-debated incised marks.

entities.name: South Asian Prehistory
entities.date_note: The era begins with the Lahuradewa environmental sequence. Some attached sites continue later, so their genuine overlap is explicitly allowed.
entities.summary: Early farming, rice cultivation, and pre-urban settlement traditions across South Asia.

entities.name: Mehrgarh
entities.date_note: A 2025 programme directly dating tooth enamel places the aceramic cemetery at 5250-4650 cal BCE, about two thousand years younger than the familiar textbook start.

alternatives.label: Classic early Mehrgarh chronology
alternatives.note: The older chronology begins the aceramic Neolithic around 7000 BCE and gives it a multi-millennial duration.

caveats.text: The often repeated 7000 BCE start is not the current direct-dating result; the 2025 tooth-enamel model makes the earliest phase roughly 2,000 years younger.

entities.summary: A key early farming settlement in the Indus borderlands whose oldest phase has been radically re-dated.

entities.name: Bhirrana
entities.date_note: The mainstream regional reading begins occupation in the fourth millennium BCE. The much older 9.5 ka sequence is an actively disputed extrapolation.

alternatives.label: Long Bhirrana chronology
alternatives.note: Sarkar and colleagues propose a Hakra phase from about 9.5 to 8 ka BP and occupation continuing to about 2.8 ka BP.

entities.summary: A Haryana settlement with a disputed claim to extraordinarily early South Asian occupation.

entities.name: Early Harappan Ravi Phase
entities.date_note: The published AMS table distinguishes raw BP measurements from its calibrated BC column and gives the phase a broad 3300-2800 BC frame.
entities.summary: The earliest well-dated phase at Harappa, before the later urban Indus city.

entities.name: Lahuradewa
entities.date_note: The environmental record begins about 10,899 cal BP and continues to the present. Archaeologists debate whether the earliest rice was domesticated or cultivated wild rice.
entities.summary: A lake-margin site in the middle Ganges plain with very early rice evidence and a long environmental sequence.

entities.name: Southeast Asian Prehistory
entities.date_note: This navigation era includes both explicitly uncalibrated conventional Hoabinhian dates and later calibrated chronologies. It cannot be read as one homogeneous dating programme.
entities.summary: The long prehistory of mainland and island Southeast Asia, including cave traditions, metal-age communities, and early human remains.

entities.name: Hoabinhian
entities.date_note: STORED AS UNCALIBRATED RADIOCARBON. The conventional 23,000-3,700 BP chronology is explicitly published as non-calibrated; it must not be converted to calendar dates automatically.

alternatives.label: Xiaodong early chronology
alternatives.note: A Yunnan rockshelter claim extends Hoabinhian to 43.5 ka and proposes a southern-China homeland.

entities.summary: A long-lived cave and rockshelter tool tradition of mainland Southeast Asia, often identified by worked pebble tools.

entities.name: Ban Chiang
entities.date_note: Directly dating human bone collagen puts the first burial phase at 1600-1450 BC and the bronze transition at 1050-955 BC; later deposits reach the Iron Age.

alternatives.label: Old long chronology
alternatives.note: The old model put the early Bronze Age at 3600 BC, based on charcoal and crushed-potsherd material now known to bias ages old.

caveats.text: Ban Chiang did not show bronze metallurgy from 3600 BC: direct bone-collagen dating revised the key transition to 1050-955 BC.

entities.summary: A northeast Thai burial site central to the re-dating of Southeast Asian bronze metallurgy.

entities.name: Niah Caves Deep Skull
entities.date_note: Re-excavation and direct U-series work support a 46-34 ka bracket; a direct cranial U-series age near 35 ka may be an underestimate.

alternatives.label: Intrusive Neolithic burial
alternatives.note: Earlier critics argued that the skull had intruded from younger Neolithic deposits rather than belonging to the Pleistocene layer.

entities.summary: A human skull from Borneo's Niah Caves, now accepted as Late Pleistocene rather than a later burial.

entities.name: Yangtze Rice Domestication
entities.date_note: STORED AS UNCALIBRATED RADIOCARBON / CALIBRATION-UNSTATED BP. The main study prints bare BP values and Chinese practice often uses uncalibrated BP; do not convert automatically.

alternatives.label: Early cultivation reading
alternatives.note: A Chinese archaeology review places cultivation at Shangshan and Hehuashan around 9,400-9,000 BP and warns that such BP is usually uncalibrated.

entities.summary: A gradual process in the lower Yangtze in which managed wild rice became fully domesticated rice.

entities.name: Americas Prehistory
entities.date_note: This navigation era starts with the re-formed Bering land bridge and extends through regionally late Archaic traditions. Some sites continue beyond it and are marked accordingly.
entities.summary: The earliest peopling of the Americas and the long sequence of regional traditions that followed.

entities.name: Bering Land Bridge
entities.date_note: Sea-level work indicates the strait was open until about 35.7 ka and the last land bridge was flooded between about 13 and 11 ka.
entities.summary: The dry land connection that intermittently linked Siberia and Alaska during the last ice age.

entities.name: Pre-Clovis Horizon
entities.date_note: Most accepted evidence falls around 16,000-15,000 years ago. Claims before the last glacial maximum remain contested rather than forming one settled horizon.

alternatives.label: Pre-LGM long chronology
alternatives.note: Some claimed sites would push occupation before 20 ka, but the combined genetic and archaeological synthesis does not accept that depth.

entities.summary: The broad label for accepted American sites older than the Clovis tool tradition.

entities.name: White Sands Footprints
entities.date_note: The original aquatic-seed dates of about 23-21 ka were independently supported by terrestrial pollen radiocarbon and quartz OSL, but objections remain active.

alternatives.label: Hard-water reservoir objection
alternatives.note: Critics argue aquatic seeds could be 7,000-10,000 years too old because they used ancient dissolved carbon from lake water.

caveats.text: The dispute has three rounds: 2021 aquatic-seed dates, a 2022 reservoir objection, and 2023 pollen plus OSL confirmation that critics still question.

entities.summary: Human footprints in New Mexico that may date to the height of the last ice age.

entities.name: Clovis Culture
entities.date_note: The modern calibrated range is about 13,050-12,750 cal BP. The underlying laboratory ages and older famous ranges are uncalibrated radiocarbon, not calendar dates.

alternatives.label: Traditional long Clovis
alternatives.note: The former 11,500-10,900 radiocarbon-year BP span was compressed by Waters and Stafford's 2007 reassessment.

caveats.text: Clovis was not a millennium-long 11,500-10,900 BCE culture: Waters and Stafford compressed the raw radiocarbon chronology, and calibration shifts it about two millennia older.

entities.summary: A short-lived North American tradition of distinctive fluted stone points.

entities.name: Folsom Culture
entities.date_note: IntCal20 Bayesian modelling gives a 95% span from 12,910-12,750 to 12,430-12,125 cal BP.
entities.summary: A bison-hunting tradition that followed Clovis across much of the North American plains.

entities.name: Paleoindian Period
entities.date_note: The continental bracket is about 13,200-11,450 cal BP, although regional period labels and boundaries vary.
entities.summary: A broad North American label for the earliest widespread post-ice-age traditions, including Clovis and Folsom.

entities.name: Archaic Period
entities.date_note: The period has no single continental end: one synthesis ends it about 3200 cal BP, while the Southwest carries it as late as AD 500.
entities.summary: A long, regionally varied North American period of adapting to post-ice-age environments, broad diets, and later early farming.

entities.name: Cactus Hill
entities.date_note: STORED AS UNCALIBRATED RADIOCARBON / CALIBRATION-UNSTATED. Available sources report 18,000-20,000 years ago but do not identify a calibration basis; the site sequence continues to contact.

caveats.text: The deepest Cactus Hill layer is not part of the settled pre-Clovis chronology; the state's defensible claim is only 'more than 15,000 years ago.'

entities.summary: A Virginia sand-dune site with a possible stone-tool layer below a Clovis level.

entities.name: Paisley Caves
entities.date_note: Human evidence reaches about 14,300 cal BP, while the cave deposits continue through historic contact. Dates and human attribution have unusually extensive testing.

caveats.text: The concern is whether soluble DNA and lipids moved into older layers; later fecal-lipid work supports the early human attribution.

entities.summary: Oregon caves with early human coprolites, basketry, and a Western Stemmed stone-point tradition.

entities.name: Sahul
entities.date_note: Human entry is modelled between about 65 and 50 ka, with a 75 ka model option. Postglacial sea rise broke the landmass apart; Bass Strait flooded about 12 ka.

alternatives.label: Genetic short chronology
alternatives.note: A genetic and archaeological short chronology places Australian arrival near 47 ka rather than the archaeological long chronology.

entities.summary: The ice-age landmass that joined Australia, Tasmania, and New Guinea when sea levels were lower.

entities.name: Madjedbebe
entities.date_note: Single-grain OSL dates the lowest artefact-bearing deposit to 65 ± 6 ka. This is a light-based age, not radiocarbon, and the locality remains culturally meaningful.

caveats.text: The challenge is not the OSL measurement itself but whether termites and other disturbance moved artefacts down into older sands.

entities.summary: A rock shelter on Mirarr Country in Arnhem Land with very early stone tools and other evidence of occupation.

entities.name: Lake Mungo
entities.date_note: Current consensus dates the burials to 40 ± 2 ka and local occupation to 50-46 ka from 25 optical ages. These are not radiocarbon dates.

alternatives.label: Thorne 1999 age
alternatives.note: A 1999 U-series/ESR and OSL study claimed 62 ± 6 ka for Mungo Man; it was superseded by the 2003 optical chronology.

caveats.text: The popular 62 ka age for Mungo Man is superseded; the current 40 ± 2 ka result comes from later OSL dating of the lunette sediments.

entities.summary: The Willandra Lakes locality of Mungo Lady and Mungo Man, two of Australia's oldest known human burials.

entities.name: Cut-Marked Bone
entities.date_note: CONTESTED, and deliberately filed as a minority claim. If the marks are butchery they predate the oldest known knapped stone by about 90,000 years and sit outside this app's 3.3 Ma scope floor. The competing reading is trampling damage, which requires no tools at all.

alternatives.label: Trampling damage, not butchery
alternatives.note: Marks attributed to sediment abrasion rather than stone tools.

caveats.text: Whether these marks were made by tools at all is unresolved; the majority reading is trampling.

entities.summary: Bones from Dikika, Ethiopia bearing marks read as stone-tool butchery, roughly 800,000 years before the oldest known stone tools.

entities.name: Structural Use of Wood
entities.date_note: Reported as at least 476+/-23 ka, by single-grain quartz OSL and post-IR IRSL on feldspars. A floor, not an estimate.

caveats.text: The claim is the oldest worked wood STRUCTURE, joined and notched, not merely the oldest worked wood.

entities.summary: Two interlocking notched logs from Kalambo Falls, Zambia: the oldest known wooden structure, built before Homo sapiens appears in the record.

entities.name: Laetoli
entities.date_note: 3.66 Ma follows the Deino (2011) recalibration of the tuffs. Filed as a site rather than as a behavioural first: this app gates its floor on knapping, and admitting bipedalism as a threshold would move the floor to 3.66 Ma on an anatomical trait rather than a manufacturing behaviour.

caveats.text: Not a single small-bodied group: the Site S prints, found in 2016, show a much larger individual at the same horizon.

entities.summary: Tanzanian site preserving the oldest confirmed hominin footprints, showing upright walking 350,000 years before the first stone tools.

entities.name: Turkana Basin
entities.date_note: Bracketed by dated tuffs: Moiti 4.10+/-0.07 Ma at the base, Silbo 0.74+/-0.01 Ma at the top, with KBS at 1.88+/-0.02 Ma between them.

caveats.text: Not one site but a multi-locality complex with different tuff sequences on each shore; it cannot be dated as a single horizon.

entities.summary: The most continuous tuff-dated hominin sequence in East Africa, spanning Koobi Fora, Nariokotome and Kokiselei on both shores of Lake Turkana.

entities.name: Hadar
entities.date_note: Argon-argon on Kada Hadar tuffs gives just under 3.18 Ma. The original 1970s potassium-argon figure of about 3 Ma +/- 200,000 was affected by contaminants and is superseded.

caveats.text: The familiar '3.2 million years' is an older rounding; the current figure is slightly younger.

entities.summary: The Afar site that produced AL 288-1, 'Lucy', the Australopithecus afarensis skeleton that made early bipedalism concrete.

entities.name: Gona
entities.date_note: Single-crystal laser fusion on the overlying tuff gives 2.53+/-0.15 Ma, with the underlying Gauss-Matuyama boundary at 2.58 Ma bracketing below.

caveats.text: No longer uniquely the oldest: Bokol Dora 1 at Ledi-Geraru dates to 2.61-2.58 Ma, so Gona is among the earliest rather than first.

entities.summary: Afar locality holding some of the oldest securely dated Oldowan stone tools, anchoring the industry's 2.6 Ma start.

entities.name: Melka Kunture
entities.date_note: The Oldowan at Garba IV is about 1.7 Ma. Whether Garba IVD holds the earliest Acheulean at 1.95 Ma is actively disputed: the claim rests on magnetostratigraphy and has been challenged as lacking a robust age model. Gombore II, later in the sequence, is securely bracketed at 0.875-0.709 Ma.

alternatives.label: Earliest Acheulean at 1.95 Ma
alternatives.note: Perini et al.: claimed earliest Acheulean technocomplex.

alternatives.label: Age model not robust
alternatives.note: Rejects the 1.9-2.0 Ma Acheulean and Oldowan occupation claims.

entities.summary: A high-altitude Ethiopian sequence running from Oldowan to Middle Stone Age, and the site of a live dispute over the world's earliest Acheulean.

entities.name: Olorgesailie
entities.date_note: Late Acheulean assemblages run 615-499 ka. The Middle Stone Age onset is most likely by about 320 ka and at least by 305 ka, which is the youngest boundary this node claims.
entities.summary: A Kenyan rift basin recording the Acheulean-to-Middle Stone Age transition, tied to Middle Pleistocene environmental instability.

entities.name: Herto
entities.date_note: Dated by argon-argon with tephra chemical correlation.

caveats.text: Not the oldest Homo sapiens: Jebel Irhoud at about 315 ka and Omo Kibish are both older.

entities.summary: Middle Awash locality that produced Homo sapiens idaltu, among the oldest near-modern human fossils.

entities.name: Bodo
entities.date_note: Weighted mean 0.64+/-0.03 Ma by laser-fusion argon-argon on vitric tephra. The age is settled; the taxonomic assignment is not.

caveats.text: Assigned to Homo heidelbergensis, or to a proposed 'Homo bodoensis'. That argument is taxonomic, not chronological.

entities.summary: Middle Awash cranium anchoring the mid-Pleistocene African record, bearing cut marks suggestive of deliberate defleshing.

entities.name: Enkapune Ya Muto
entities.date_note: STORED AS UNCALIBRATED RADIOCARBON. Excavation reports give bare BP without stating a calibration basis, so these are not calendar dates. The blade industry is reported as at least 46,000 and possibly 50,000 years old; the ostrich-eggshell beads at about 40,000.

caveats.text: Usually summarised as '40,000-year-old beads', which hides the older and far more contested claim about the blade industry beneath them.

entities.summary: Kenyan rock shelter with a claim to the earliest Later Stone Age blade technology in Africa, and the oldest directly dated ornaments anywhere.

entities.name: Kabwe
entities.date_note: 299+/-25 ka at two sigma, from direct uranium-series dating of the skull itself. Other bones from the assemblage span roughly 301-102 ka, which points to multiple individuals or reworked deposits; the site was destroyed by quarrying, so several associated dates are minimum ages only.

caveats.text: Routinely given as about 500,000 years old for most of the twentieth century. Direct dating in 2020 made it roughly 200,000 years younger.

entities.summary: Zambian cranium once called Homo rhodesiensis, and the clearest case in African palaeoanthropology of a textbook number being wrong by 200,000 years.

entities.name: Sterkfontein
entities.date_note: Two independent methods disagree by over a million years for the SAME deposits. Cosmogenic 26Al/10Be burial dating puts Little Foot at 3.67+/-0.16 Ma and Member 4 at 3.41-3.61 Ma; U-Pb flowstone, ESR and palaeomagnetic work puts Member 4 at 2.61-2.07 Ma and Little Foot at 2.17+/-0.17 Ma. Unresolved as of 2024. The span stored here deliberately covers both, and neither end should be read as a settled figure.

alternatives.label: Cosmogenic burial dating
alternatives.note: Little Foot 3.67+/-0.16 Ma; Member 4 3.41-3.49 Ma.

caveats.text: Popular accounts quote 3.67 Ma for Little Foot as settled; a U-Pb counter-chronology roughly 1.5 million years younger is still live.

entities.summary: Cradle of Humankind cave system holding 'Mrs Ples' and 'Little Foot', and the most actively contested chronology in African palaeoanthropology.

entities.name: Swartkrans
entities.date_note: Member 1 Lower Bank at 2.22+/-0.09 Ma by cosmogenic isochron burial dating, agreeing within one sigma with a U-Pb flowstone age of 2.25+/-0.08 Ma. Member 3 at 0.96+/-0.09 Ma.

caveats.text: Older faunal-correlation ages are superseded by isochron cosmogenic and U-Pb dating; sources quoting only faunal ages are out of date.

entities.summary: Cradle of Humankind cave with the earliest well-dated Paranthropus robustus and among the oldest Oldowan tools in southern Africa.

entities.name: Rising Star Cave
entities.date_note: A combined 236-335 ka estimate: OSL on sediment with uranium-thorium and palaeomagnetism on flowstones for the older bound, US-ESR on teeth for the younger. The age is settled; the claim of deliberate burial is not.

caveats.text: Its primitive anatomy suggested a Pliocene age, but naledi is Middle Pleistocene and contemporary with early Homo sapiens.

entities.summary: The Dinaledi Chamber, source of the Homo naledi fossils, whose surprisingly young age placed a small-brained hominin alongside early Homo sapiens.

entities.name: Sibudu Cave
entities.date_note: Single-grain OSL throughout. Post-Howiesons Poort, late and final MSA phases have weighted means of 58.5+/-1.4, 47.7+/-1.4 and 38.6+/-1.9 ka, separated by two occupational hiatuses. Whether the Howiesons Poort was a short episode or persisted to about 50 ka is an open regional debate.
entities.summary: KwaZulu-Natal shelter with the finest-resolution Middle Stone Age sequence in southern Africa, from pre-Still Bay through Howiesons Poort to the final MSA.

entities.name: Pinnacle Point
entities.date_note: PP5-6 re-dated in 2025 by single-grain OSL with Bayesian age modelling over 169 samples, giving about 92-49 ka. Individual units run from 96+/-6 ka down to 52+/-3 ka.
entities.summary: Southern Cape caves with early evidence for marine resource use, heat treatment of stone and pigment, and one of the most precisely dated MSA sequences.

entities.name: Diepkloof Rock Shelter
entities.date_note: The engraving tradition is placed securely between 55 and 65 ka by OSL, with a thermoluminescence estimate of 61+/-4 ka for one layer boundary. A later paper from the same group gives a much wider 100-52 ka range; that discrepancy is unreconciled, so the narrower sourced window is used here.
entities.summary: Western Cape shelter whose engraved ostrich eggshell containers are among the earliest deliberately produced graphic marks known.

entities.name: Apollo 11 Cave
entities.date_note: OSL gives 29.4+/-1.4 ka and the uppermost MSA layer 29.8+/-1.1 ka. An AMS radiocarbon date of 29.0+/-0.4 ka BP accompanies these, but the published report does not state whether it is calibrated, so the OSL ages are used as the boundary and the radiocarbon is not converted. A frequently quoted 25,500-23,500 BC almost certainly reflects that calibration ambiguity rather than a competing measurement.

caveats.text: The two circulating figures are dating conventions, probably calibrated versus uncalibrated, not rival scientific claims.

entities.summary: Namibian shelter holding seven painted stone plaques, four figurative, among the oldest known figurative art in Africa.

entities.name: Jebel Irhoud
entities.date_note: 315+/-34 ka, a weighted average from thermoluminescence on heated flints cross-checked by uranium-series and ESR on teeth. The Irhoud 3 mandible dates separately to 286+/-32 ka.

caveats.text: Originally classified as archaic or Neanderthal-related and dated to about 40,000 years; both the age and the classification were wrong.

entities.summary: Moroccan site holding the oldest securely dated Homo sapiens fossils, which moved the species' origin back by roughly 100,000 years.

entities.name: Taforalt
entities.date_note: The Iberomaurusian appears from at least 21,160 cal BP, after a Middle Stone Age industry persisting to about 24.5 ka cal BP and an occupational gap. Bayesian-modelled from 54 AMS dates. At least 34 burials are directly dated to between 15,077 and 13,892 cal BP.

caveats.text: Older work spread the burials across 23,000-10,800 BP; direct AMS dating narrows the burial episode to about 1,200 years.

entities.summary: The most extensively radiocarbon-dated Later Stone Age site in North Africa, and the location of the continent's oldest known cemetery.

entities.name: Wadi Kubbaniya
entities.date_note: STORED AS UNCALIBRATED RADIOCARBON. The published site dates are conventional BP without a stated calibration basis, so they are not calendar years. A later synthesis of the broader aggradation sequence gives about 25,650-22,650 cal BP, which refers to different stratigraphic units rather than contradicting these.

caveats.text: The barley, lentils and wheat found here were shown by AMS dating to be modern contaminants. This is not an early-agriculture site.

entities.summary: Late Palaeolithic sites near Aswan, once thought to hold the world's earliest cereal cultivation, and a cautionary case in contamination.

entities.name: Gobero
entities.date_note: Kiffian hunter-fisher-gatherers 9.6-7.4 kBP, then a gap of about 800 years, then Tenerian pastoralists 6.6-4.8 kBP. Recalibrated to IntCal20, which narrowed the gap originally reported as roughly a millennium.
entities.summary: The largest and oldest known Stone Age cemetery in the Sahara, preserving two distinct Holocene populations either side of a drought.

entities.name: Capsian Culture
entities.date_note: About 10,000 to 6,000 cal BP. The Typical-to-Upper Capsian transition falls near the 8,200 cal BP cold event, after which pressure technique dominates.

caveats.text: Not purely a foraging tradition throughout: pottery appears in a hunter-gatherer context by 8,000 cal BP and herding by 7,400 cal BP.

entities.summary: Epipalaeolithic to early Neolithic tradition of the eastern Maghreb, known for its shell-and-ash mound sites and later pressure-flaked bladelets.

entities.name: Khartoum Mesolithic
entities.date_note: Dated between 8800-8500 and 5000 BCE. Note that at the type site Esh-Shaheinab the Mesolithic levels were never directly dated at all; their placement rests on typological cross-dating of the Dotted Wavy Line horizon.

caveats.text: Distinct from the later Khartoum Neolithic, which is a stock-keeping and cultivating tradition, not merely a later phase of this one.

entities.summary: Pottery-using but pre-agricultural hunter-fisher-gatherers of the central Nile, known for wavy-line and dotted-wavy-line ceramics.

entities.name: Fayum Neolithic
entities.date_note: About 5700-4200 cal BC, preceded by the Fayum Epipalaeolithic (Qarunian) at roughly 7100-6000 cal BC. Different lines of evidence give different figures: about 5800 BC for earliest cereal cultivation from lake cores, 5400 BC for the first domestic animals, and 4650-4350 BC for the Kom K and Kom W settlements.

caveats.text: The three commonly quoted dates refer to different evidence at different locations in the oasis and should not be merged into one.

entities.summary: One of the earliest well-documented farming and herding sequences in the Nile Valley, following the Qarunian foragers of the same oasis.

entities.name: Ishango
entities.date_note: STORED AS UNCALIBRATED RADIOCARBON, and genuinely unresolved. Local volcanic activity altered the carbon reservoir and no charcoal was available for cross-checking. Three incompatible figures circulate: roughly 8,500-11,000 years from the original assessment, about 20,000 from later review, and about 22,000 attributed to Alison Brooks. The stored span covers them rather than choosing between them.

alternatives.label: Original assessment, 9000-6500 BCE
alternatives.note: Earliest published framing; radiocarbon compromised by volcanism.

alternatives.label: About 22,000 years
alternatives.note: Third figure in circulation, attributed to Alison Brooks.

caveats.text: Popular writing gives a confident '20,000 years'; the technical literature calls the radiocarbon unreliable and offers three figures.

entities.summary: A Semliki River site in the DRC, famous for a notched bone sometimes read as an early tally device, and unusually hard to date.

entities.name: Cattle Herding in Africa
entities.date_note: Dated archaeozoologically and cross-checked against population genomics rather than by a single radiometric method on the animals themselves. A 2017 reassessment argues the long-standing hypothesis of independent early Holocene domestication in northeast Africa should be abandoned.

alternatives.label: Independent African domestication, 10,000-8,000 BP
alternatives.note: Long-dominant model; the eastern Saharan Bos are now read as aurochs.

caveats.text: Nabta Playa's early Holocene cattle bones are widely cited as early domestication; they are argued to be hunted wild aurochs.

entities.summary: The oldest uncontroversial domestic cattle in Africa, in Egypt's Western Desert -- introduced from the Near East rather than domesticated locally.

entities.name: African Cereal Domestication
entities.date_note: Sorghum domestication is under way in eastern Sudan by the fourth millennium BC on Butana Group pottery impressions; pearl millet is attested in the Tilemsi Valley by about 2500-2000 BC, with a single directly dated grain at 2621-2464 BCE.

caveats.text: Neither crop has a domestication date: both were gradual processes running centuries, with cultivation preceding morphological domestication.

entities.summary: Pearl millet in the West African Sahel and sorghum in eastern Sudan: two independent African domestications of indigenous cereals.

entities.name: Bantu Homeland Phase
entities.date_note: Dated by historical linguistics and ceramic typology cross-referenced with population genetics, not by a single method. Two syntheses disagree by 1,000 to 2,000 years on when proto-Bantu itself formed: 6,000-7,000 to 4,000-5,000 years ago, versus 3000-2000 BCE.

alternatives.label: Proto-Bantu forms 3000-2000 BCE
alternatives.note: Cambridge synthesis; Grassfields ancestral group predates 3000 BCE.

caveats.text: The Bantu expansion was not a sudden migration; this homeland phase alone ran more than two millennia before any outward spread.

entities.summary: The long local development of proto-Bantu in the Cameroon Grassfields, before any outward expansion across the continent.

entities.name: Nok Culture
entities.date_note: An early phase begins around the middle of the second millennium BC; the main phase with terracottas and iron production runs from the 9th to the 4th century BC. Iron-smelting dates are genuinely imprecise: the earliest Nok furnaces calibrate to about 800-550 BCE, but a radiocarbon calibration plateau near 2450 BP makes this window resistant to sharpening by more dating.

alternatives.label: Taruga furnace determinations, 920-280 BCE
alternatives.note: Four raw samples from one site spanning nearly a millennium.

caveats.text: Single confident dates for 'the start of iron smelting' hide a calibration plateau that no amount of further dating will resolve.

entities.summary: Central Nigerian culture producing sub-Saharan Africa's earliest large-scale sculptural tradition, and some of its earliest iron smelting.
